Metagenome metabolic analysis revealing the
mechanism of simultaneous methanogenesis,
aerobic methane oxidation and denitriﬁcation
(SMAMOD) in a microaerobic up-ﬂow sludge
bed bioﬁlm reactor
Zhou Xin,a,b*
Yin Zeyang,a,b Ge Daling,a,b Wang Gongleia,b and
Zhang Weia,b
Abstract
BACKGROUND: Improved denitriﬁcation with methane as alternative electron donor is regarded as a promising low-cost
approach for organic nitrate-containing wastewater treatment. However, in situ capture of methane released from a methano-
genic system for enhancing nitrogen removal seems to be scarcely reported. The applications of simultaneous denitriﬁcation,
methanogenesis, and aerobic methane oxidation coupled to denitriﬁcation provide the possibility for solving the challenging
issue.
RESULTS: In this study, simultaneous methanogenesis, aerobic methane oxidation, and denitriﬁcation (SMAMOD) was ﬁrstly
established in a microaerobic up-ﬂow sludge bed bioﬁlm reactor (MUSBBR) treating high-strength synthetic wastewater with
2000 mg L−1 Chemical oxygen demand (COD) and 400 mg L−1 nitrate. The operation demonstrated 98.8% COD, 98.8% NO3
−-N,
and 93.5% TN removals were stably obtained. Microbial community found the coexistence and cooperation of Methanothrix as
methanogens, Methylogaea as aerobic methanotrophs, as well as facultative denitriﬁcation genera in SMAMOD system. Gene proﬁl-
ing demonstrated key functional genes involved in aerobic and anaerobic fermentation, methanogenesis and aerobic methane oxi-
dation, as well as nitrate reduction induced by nitrate reductase systems. In organic oxygen-limited biotransformation, glucose was
degraded mainly through aerobic respiration, anaerobic fermentation into methane by decarboxylation of acetic acid, and further
methane aerobic oxidation pathways, while acetate- and methanol-denitriﬁcation and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium
pathways participated in the nitrogen bioconversion. Further, the metabolic mechanism of SMAMOD might be unraveled by spatial
interactions of key metagenomes in core microbial consortiums in the MUSBBR reactor.
CONCLUSION: The study offers valuable metagenomic insights into SMAMOD as a potentially compact process for sustainable
treatment of high-strength organic nitrate-containing wastewater.

Keywords: SMAMOD; aerobic methane oxidation; metagenomics; functional genes; metabolic mechanism
INTRODUCTION
A large amount of nitrate (over 200 mg NO3
−-N/L) is generally
contained in complex high-strength organic wastewaters pro-
duced from the dairy, explosive, fertilizer, and nuclear industries,
as well as landﬁll industries,1 so nitrogen removal needs to be
considered during conventional anaerobic treatment of organic
matter.2 In tradition, a separate denitriﬁcation process is often
indispensable after anaerobic digestion (AD) treatment of these
wastewaters.3 However, this practice seems not economic and
sustainable. For one thing, the supply of external carbons is
needed for denitriﬁcation, because most of the biodegradable
COD is removed beforehand by anaerobic treatment, thus
increasing the subsequent removal of residual organics and oper-
ational costs. Another point is that some of this methane, espe-
cially dissolved methane which is difﬁcult to recycle, may lead to
powerful greenhouse gas (GHG) effects if improperly managed.4
Therefore, it is essential to eliminate nitrogen and dissolved meth-
ane from organic- and nitrate-containing wastewater during AD
treatment.

Simultaneous denitriﬁcation and methanogenesis (SDM) was a
feasible alternative to post-denitriﬁcation through introducing
denitriﬁcation into the methanogenic reactor.5 In the single
SDM reactor, a fraction of COD is able to be utilized as electron
donor for nitrate reduction without installing an additional deni-
triﬁcation unit. Until now, SDM has been achieved in anaerobic
bafﬂed reactor, 6 anaerobic up-ﬂow ﬁlter,7 up-ﬂow anaerobic
sludge blanket,8 and expanded granular sludge bed.9 However,
the competition of organic matter between denitriﬁers and
methanogens largely leads to affect SDM performance.5,8 Over
the past decades, methane oxidation as a newly global carbon
pathway has been extensively discovered in natural water envi-
ronments, 10 which plays a signiﬁcant role in methane emission
reduction. Under anaerobic or aerobic environments, diverse
groups of methyl-oxidizing bacteria (methanotrophs) allow meth-
ane oxidation.11 In contrast to anaerobic methanotrophic bacteria
(AnMB), aerobic methanotrophic bacteria (AMB) demonstrate
intrinsic advantages with faster growth rate, stronger metabolic
ability, and less environment sensibility.12 Aerobic methane oxi-
dation (AMO) means that methane is enabled to be oxidized into
some organic intermediates (such as methanol), which can supply
alternative organic carbons for denitriﬁcation, known as aerobic
methane oxidation coupled to denitriﬁcation (AME-D).13 So far,
AME-D process has been investigated in some bioreactors with
external methane gas supplied by either pumping aeration14 or
membrane aeration15 into the liquid.
If some portions of excessive methane difﬁcult to collect and
reuse are capable of being utilized by AMB, it is more likely to
improve nitrogen removal capacity and mitigate GHG potential
by integrating AMO and denitriﬁcation into a single methano-
genic reactor. Hence, from the viewpoint of availability and econ-
omy, in situ utilization of methane generated in methanation
systems will be undoubtedly more attractive to the application
of AME-D. Due to the low solubility of methane in the liquid
phase,16 however, high methanogenesis efﬁciency should be
maintained to guarantee enough capture of methane for possible
in-site AMO. Previous literatures17,18 have reported the effective-
ness of microaerobic pretreatment for improving methane yield,
since facultative in-situ can rapidly hydrolyze organic matter into
small molecule organics, such as volatile fatty acids (VFAs), in favor
of the growth of methane-producing bacteria (MPB). Moreover,
microaerophilic maintenance also serves as a pivotal link between
AMO and denitriﬁcation for achieving AME-D. Based on these,
methanogenesis, methane aerobic oxidation, and denitriﬁcation
are expected to simultaneously (SMAMOD) occur in one micro-
aerobic system.
As an effective tool to deeply understand the fundamentals of
complex wastewater biological treatment processes, 16S rDNA-
based metagenomics were used for identifying interactions of
the mixed microbiomes and determining key functional gene
metabolic pathways driving biochemical reactions.19,20 Therefore,
the present study mainly aims to reveal the underlying metabolic
mechanism of SMAMOD using metagenomics based on the suc-
cessful build-up of SMAMOD in a single microaerobic up-ﬂow
sludge bed bioﬁlm reactor (MUSBBR).
MATERIAL AND METHODS
Reactor start-up and operation
A lab-scale MUSBBR system was used in Fig. 1. The 17 L effective
volume system consisted of the main reaction body (9 L) and a
three-phase separator (8 L). The main body included a sludge
bed combined with a packing bed ﬁlled with about 25% (v/v)
PU sponge as biocarrier. The seeding sludge was obtained from
a municipal wastewater treatment plant (Jingzhong city, Shanxi
province) and inoculated into the reactor at 2:1 mixing ratio of
thickening sludge (MLSS: 15.76 g L−1) and aerobic activated
sludge (MLSS: 7.47 g L−1). In this study, synthetic wastewater con-
tains tap water and speciﬁc compositions (L) as follows: 2134 mg
glucose, 0–6071.4 mg NaNO3, 50 mg NaHCO3, 309.7 mg NaH2PO4,
55.5 mg CaCl2 and trace element solution (5 g EDTA, 2 g
FeCl3·4H2O, 0.2 g CoCl2·6H2O, 0.5 g MnCl2·4H2O, 0.03 mg
CuCl2·2H2O, 0.05 g ZnCl2, 0.1 g Na2SeO3, 0.05 g NiCl2·6H2O,
0.09 g Na2MoO4, 0.05 g H3BO4 per liter). To ensure mesophilic
methane production, the wastewater temperature was controlled
at 35°C by a heating controller and inﬂuent pH was adjusted to
7.221 by adding HCl (1 mM). During the start-up, the reactor was
only fed with high-strength organic wastewater (2000 mg L−1
COD) without nitrate. After a 48-day stable methanation start-
up, nitrate (0–1000 mg L−1 NO3
−-N) was gradually added into
the feeding. According to a preliminary experiment, the optimal
performance
occurred
at
the
corresponding
inﬂuent
COD/NO3
−-N (C/N) of 5. The pre-aeration before the feeding ﬂo-
wed into the reactor was undertaken to maintain microaerobic
conditions. Dissolved oxygen (DO) and oxidation–reduction
potential (ORP) levels were 0.2 mg L−1 and −340 mv, respec-
tively. The hydraulic retention time (HRT) was ﬁxed at 2 days dur-
ing the experiment period.
NH4
+-N, NO2
−-N, NO3
−-N and COD of the efﬂuent samples after
0.45 μm membrane ﬁltering were determined by cuvette kits test
(HACH LANGE LTD, US). Total nitrogen (TN) is the sum of NH4
+-N
and NOx
−-N. pH, DO, and ORP were monitored by a portable anal-
ysis meter (WTW 3420, Germany). CH4 and CO2 gas samples over
the headspace were analyzed by a gas chromatograph (GC-
4000A, China) equipped with ﬂame ionization detector (FID) and
thermal conductivity detector (TCD), respectively.
Sample collection and DNA extraction
Three different sludge samples with 10 mL each were collected
from top, middle, and bottom sample ports from the sludge

bed, and nine bio-carriers were collected from top, middle, and
bottom sample ports from the packing bed on day 32. All the
sludge samples were directly mixed and the mixture was put into
a 2 mL centrifuge tube for DNA extraction, while all the carriers
were cut and mixed. Bioﬁlm surface microorganisms were
ensured to be contacted using the lysate to release more DNA.
Speciﬁc DNA extraction steps were according to OMEGA kit
E.Z.N. Atm Mag-BindSoil DNA Kit's usage instructions (http://
omegabiotek.com/store/production/soil-dna-kit/).
High-throughput sequencing
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) ampliﬁcation was carried out.
16S rDNA ampliﬁcation area for V3-V4 domains, PCR primers for
bacteria incorporating Miseq sequencing platform V3-V4 univer-
sal primers 341 F primer: CCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTGCC
TACGGGNGGCWGCAG, 805 R primer: GACTGGAGTTCCTTGGC
ACCCGAGAATTCCAGACTACHVGGGTATCTAATCC. The Qubit 3.0
DNA testing kit was used to precisely quantify the recovered
DNA. When mixed with the same amount, 10 ng of DNA was taken
from each sample, and Illumina Miseq high-throughput sequenc-
ing was performed by Sangon bioengineering co., LTD (Shanghai,
China). The compiled sequences were compared with the rRNA
gene sequences in the GenBank using NCBI BLAST program.
The sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units
(OTUs) with the 97% similarity threshold.
Bioinformatic analysis
The raw image data ﬁle obtained by Illumina Miseq™was trans-
formed into the original sequencing sequence by CASAVA Base
Calling analysis and stored in FASTQ (fq) format ﬁle, containing
the sequence information and its corresponding quality informa-
tion. To pretreat the raw data, it was necessary to remove the
primer joint sequence, then splice the paired reads into a
sequence according to the overlapping relationship between
the PE reads, then identify and distinguish the samples according
to the barcode technical label sequence to obtain each sample
data. Finally, the quality of each sample data was controlled and
ﬁltrated to obtain the valid data. Subsequently, the unampliﬁed
region sequence in the pre-processed sequence was removed
using Usearch, followed by sequencing error correction of the
sequence, and the uchime was used to identify the chimera. The
chimeric removal sequences with the database representative
sequence were compared by BLAST. To obtain the metabolic
information, PICRUSt software was used to predict the functional
gene composition in the samples obtained by 16 s sequencing to
analyze the functional differences between different samples. The
protein sequences of predicted genes were compared by Kyoto
Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database (https://
www.kegg.jp/).
To explore organic and nitrogen metabolisms, associated func-
tional genes involved in metabolic pathways were identiﬁed in
detail according to protein sequences predictions using KEGG
database.22 Key genes for fermentation chieﬂy include glucose
kinase (glk), glucose phosphate isomerase (pgi), phosphate glyce-
rate mutase (gpm), pyruvate formate lyase (pﬂ), pyruvate kinase
(PK), pyruvate dehydrogenase (pdh), pyruvate ferredoxin oxidore-
ductase (por), and 2-oxoacid ferredoxin oxidoreductase subunit
(oor). Key enzymes involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle
are
citrate
synthase
(CS),
isocitrate
dehydrogenase
(IDH),
2-oxoglutarate ferredoxin oxidoreductase subunit (kor), and
malate dehydrogenase (mdh). Key methane-producing and
methane-oxidizing genes involve acetokinase (ack), phosphoric
acetyltransferase (pta), acetyl-coa synthetase (acs), CODH/ACS
complex subunit (cdh), tetrahydromethanopterin methyltransfer-
ase (mtr), methyl coenzyme M reductase (mcr), heterodisulﬁde
reductase (hdr), F420 non-reducing hydrogenase (mvh), methane
oxygenase (mmo), alcohol oxidase (MOX), formaldehyde dehy-
drogenase (fdh), formic acid dehydrogenase (FDH, fdw, fds) and
glutathione dehydrogenase (frm). 23 In the nitrogen cycle, key
enzymes include: nitrate reductase (nar, nap), nitrite reductase
(nirKS), nitric oxide reductase (nor), nitrous oxide reductase
(nos), nitrite reductase (nrf, nirBD), assimilatory nitrate reductase
(nas, nirA), and nitrogenase (nif). 24 These genetic results were
converged into KEGG metabolic networks to reveal metabolic
pathways and their roles in carbon and nitrogen cycles.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Reactor performance
Figure 2 shows the system performance under the inﬂuent
400 mg L−1 NO3
−-N. Under the steady-state condition, the system
averagely removed as high as 98.8% COD with a high methane
recovery up to 664.5 mL day−1, indicating stably efﬁcient metha-
nation efﬁciency. Meanwhile, nearly 99% nitrate removal rate was
also achieved. In the efﬂuent, ammonia nitrogen was basically in

the form of total nitrogen, while nitrate/nitrite nitrogen was rather
low. As such, the corresponding average TN removal efﬁciency
reached up to 93.5%. In theory, it was not possible to achieve high
methane yield at such a low C/N ratio (<10), since most of the
organics would be consumed for denitriﬁcation in SDM systems.5
Yet this could not explain desirable methane production. There-
fore, we inferred that in a robust methanogenic system, stepwise
nitrate addition had a minor effect on methanogenic activity.
Moreover, microaerobic conditions accelerated a large accumula-
tion of organic acids and resulted in a sharp fall of the pH level
(<7), thereby fermentation bacteria outgrew denitriﬁers at low
pH levels. These factors led to the precedence of methanogenesis
over denitriﬁcation in our system. But if only methanogenesis
occurs, excellent nitrogen removal seems impossible. Thus, we
could conclude the signiﬁcant role of methane in nitrogen
removal promotion via aerobic methane oxidation coupled with
denitriﬁcation (AME-D), when organic substrates severely lacked.
Based on this assumption, most of the glucose should be fermen-
tatively used for methane transformation instead of denitriﬁca-
tion. Then, methane in situ generated in a methanation reactor
was oxidized by aerobic methane-oxidizers into oxidative prod-
ucts, such as methanol for nitration reduction under oxygen-
limited conditions. Besides, nitrate being directly reduced to
ammonia via DNRA, frequently happened in SDM systems fed
with glucose.5,25 That could explain a bit of ammonia left in the
ﬁnal efﬂuent. Given these factors, we forecast that methanogen-
esis, aerobic methane oxidation, and denitriﬁcation should be
concurrently developed in a single methane-producing system
through integrating SMD and AME-D.
Microbial community analysis
To identify the functional bacteria in the SMAMOD system, the
sludge and bioﬁlm samples were respectively taken from the
sludge and packing bed for microbial community analysis based
on 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The count of OTUs was found to
be 5450 for the sludge sample and 4779 for the bioﬁlm sample.
Also, the Shannon index of 5.61 was in sludge, while 5.14 in bio-
ﬁlm. These data imply that the sludge bed has more complex
and diverse community structures than the packing bed. At phyla
level, Proteobacteria were largest, followed by Chloroﬂex and Bac-
teroidetes. These major phyla suggest the dominance of faculta-
tive heterotrophs responsible for organic matter and nitrate
transformations. Furthermore, Euryarchaeota were also discov-
ered in either sludge or bioﬁlm samples, certifying the presence
of methanogenic microorganisms.26 Figure 3 further displays
microbial compositions at genus level. Among the total of
389 genera, some genera Thauera, Comamonas, Rhizobium, and
Rhodobacter as members of chemoheterotrophs were shared in
both samples. Remarkably, Methanothrix, as a common methano-
gen that thrives in acetate-rich environments27 was discovered in
both two samples, denoting widespread development of metha-
nogenesis throughout the reactor. For the whole population
structure, however, there was some evident differentiations
between two samples. It was interesting to note that Methylogaea,
belonging to aerobic methanotrophs28,29 overwhelmingly existed
in the bioﬁlm (0.92%), whereas almost none existed in sludge. This
exciting discovery veriﬁed the potential of AMO in the system.
AMO might be encouraged by the prolonged contact time of
methane and an enlarged low-oxygen micro-environment pro-
vided by a packing bed. Furthermore, Methyloversatilis (3.4%), as
an alcoholic denitrifer30 also typically found in bioﬁlm, conﬁrms
methanol produced from AMO for denitriﬁcation via AME-D.
Despite the richness of Acinetobacter, Saccharibacteria with strong
degrading capacity of complex organic matter31,32 were far
higher in sludge than those in bioﬁlm. This might be because aer-
obic and anaerobic glucose degradation initially occurred at the
sludge bed of the micro-aerobic system, where the organic sub-
strates were quite abundant. Other dominant facultative genera
Thaura, Comamonas, Flavobacterium, Longilinea, Azospira, and
Thermomonas were also extensively identiﬁed. These nitrogen-
cycle-associated microbes were closely related to nitrogen
removal. In general, the 16S rRNA gene sequencing consequences
gave strong evidence for microbial co-existence-induced SMA-
MOD in a MUSBBR system.
Functional gene proﬁling
Further functional gene proﬁling during the organic matter and
nitrate biocoversion in the system is illustrated as Fig. 4. As clearly
shown, substantial fermentation genes and subunits were domi-
nant in both samples, while more associated genes numbers were
observed in the sludge. That was associated with the predomi-
nance of fermentative bacterium carrying these genes with the
ability of degrading glucose. Particularly, a higher abundance of
anaerobic and aerobic fermentation functional genes implied fur-
ther anaerobic conversion of glycolysis products to methane as
well as a few its aerobic degradation to CO2 via TCA cycle. More-
over, the abundance of reductase subunit (hdr) in sludge was up
to 29754, which was much higher than that in bioﬁlm (15832).
This indicated that methane production ﬁrstly took place in the
sludge bed. Due to the presence of functional genes related to
the conversion of acetic acid into methane, acetotrophic metha-
nogenesis was proved in this study, in line with the observation
of Methanothrix. In addition, vast key genes mmo with the poten-
tial function of methane oxidation33 were signiﬁcantly monitored

in the bioﬁlm. The whole detection of genes (mmo and MOX,34

Compared with carbon metabolism genes, nitrogen-transfor-
mation-associated functional genes were relatively low. Among
them, a higher abundance of nitrate reductase (nar) with more
than 5000 was found either in the sludge or bioﬁlm, indicating a
high nitrate removal rate in the study. However, the quantity of
nitrate reductase (nap) in bioﬁlm (877) was much lower than that
in sludge (1933). This might be associated with the biodiversity of
nitrate-reducing bacteria with different metabolism ways. In
terms of nitrite reduction, a key gene (nirKS) was detected with
similar abundances between the two samples showing further
biochemical transformation from NO2
−-N to NO. Furthermore,
nitrite reductase (nrf) able to catalyze DNRA35 with relatively high
abundances was noticed in our methanogenic system. A quite
small number of assimilatory nitrate reductase and nitrogenase
was also found, which participated in the nitrogen bioconversion.
The identiﬁcation of these functional genomes might constitute
the complete nitrogen metabolism network.
Metabolic pathways
In this study, metagenomic analysis was used to reveal further
metabolic pathways for understanding the transformation behav-
ior of organics and nitrogen. In the organic metabolism given in
Fig. 5, glycolysis was the ﬁrst step, in which glucose was decom-
posed into pyruvic acid via Embden-Meyerhof pathway (EMP)
by a series of genes. And then key genes participating both in
the aerobic and anaerobic degradation of pyruvic acid were dis-
tinguished because of the microaerobic environment. In the aero-
bic fermentation of pyruvic acid, acetyl coenzyme A was directly
formed and was then completely degraded into CO2 through tri-
carboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. But in the anaerobic fermentation,
pyruvic acid was ﬁrstly catalyzed into VFA (including acetic acid)
by pyruvic acid lyase (pﬂ), and then into acetyl coenzyme A as a
core precursor to methane production by genes (acs, ack and
pta).36,37 Under the action of gene cdh, acetyl coenzyme A was
combined with 5,6,7,8-tetrahydromethanopterin (THM(S)PT) to
form coenzyme M (CoM) and methyl-CoM under the role of gene
mtr. Finally, methane could be yielded by reduction of methyl-
CoM by key gene mcr. Besides, a few methyl-CoM might be
reduced to Com-S-S-CoB and then back to CoM again by genes
hdr and mvh, both of which continued to participate in the meth-
ane production pathway.38 This metagenomic pathway informa-
tion strongly indicated methane production from acetate
oxidative decarboxylation in this study.
After the ﬁnish of methanogenesis, methane was at ﬁrst oxidized
into methanol by the action of methane oxygenase (mmo) under
microaerophilic conditons.39 We could convincingly believe that
AMO was responsible for the CH4 bioconversion. Afterwards, meth-
anol was mainly further oxidized into formaldehyde and formate
based on the detection of alcohol oxidase (MOX) and formalde-
hyde dehydrogenase (fdhA, gfa). Complete mineralization might
also be included by gene (FDH and fds). A sequence of biochemical
reaction steps indicates complete AMO-induced40 enzyme systems
in our study. We also tracked that a fraction of byproducts, e.g.
acetic acid and methanol (respectively, from fermentation and
AMO steps), were also utilized for possible denitriﬁcation.41 Owing
to these bioconversion pathways, glucose was thoroughly trans-
formed into biogas (CH4 and CO2).
Figure 6 reveals nitrogen metabolic pathways. Distinctly, com-
plete nitrate-nitrogen bioconversion routes are composed of
nitrate reduction to nitrite, nitrite reduction to nitrogen oxide,
nitrite reduction to ammonia, assimilatory nitrate (nitrite) reduc-
tion, and nitrogen ﬁxation in our system. Even though the ﬁrst
step started at the NO3
−-N reduction to NO2
−-N, the involved
genes were not the same. Dissimilatory nitrate reduction (denitri-
ﬁcation and DNRA) was driven by genes nap and nar, while gene
nas executed assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Based on Fig. 4,
the total abundances of nar and nap were always higher than nas,
implying dissimilatory reduction pathways dominated in nitrogen
removal.
Subsequently,
further
nitrite
reduction
reactions
included three different types of pathways, according to metage-
nomic analysis: 1 denitriﬁcation: NO2
−-N underwent a three-step
reduction reaction into dinitrogen in the role of nirKS, nor, and
nos, followed by NH4
+-N formation through nitrogen ﬁxation
(NF) gene (nif); 2 DNRA: NO2
−-N could be directly reduced to
NH4
+-N with the participation of nirBD and nrf; 3 ANR: NO2
−-N
assimilatory reduction to NH4
+-N was executed by gene nirA.
These also correctly explained that an extremely high nitrogen
removal rate along with a fraction of ammonia remained in the
ﬁnal efﬂuent in Fig. 2(a).
Implication of SMAMOD process
Figure 7 indicates a comprehensive metagenomic description of
organics and nitrogen metabolism networks to explore the possi-
ble mechanism of SMAMOD in the USBBR system. In this graph,

left and right heatmaps represent the relative abundance of key
functional bacteria and genes in the sludge and bioﬁlm. As
shown, glycolysis was the ﬁrst step during glucose biotransforma-
tion. Masses of aerobic and anaerobic facultative bacteria (Acine-
tobacter, Saccaribacteria, Longilinea, Levilinea) as hydrolysis and
acidiﬁcation core genera were primarily found in the sludge

was able to be readily decomposed by these organic-degrading

Determination of key functional genes in the sludge bed suggests
anaerobic fermentation was a main pathway for further transfor-
mation of glycolysis products like pyruvic acid base on the heat-
map, although its aerobic respiration via TCA cycle also existed
in microaerobic hydrolysis process. Based on the anaerobic fer-
mentation of pyruvic acid, acetyl coenzyme A, as an indispensable
intermediate, participated in the formation of coenzyme M for
methane-synthesis metabolic reaction through the action of key
genes (mtr, mcr, hdr). As such, methane was successfully gener-
ated through decarboxylation of acetic acid, which was also con-
ﬁrmed by the deﬁnite identiﬁcation of Methanothrix as a typical
acetotrophic methanogen27 in this study. Meanwhile, only a por-
tion of acetic acids could be provided as a carbon source for
denitriﬁers due to their activity inhibition at signiﬁcantly deceased
pH levels.
In the bioﬁlm phase, even if glucose was rather scarce, anaerobic
micro-environments further sped up bioconversion of residual
micromolecular intermediates such as organic acids (including ace-
tate) into methane, when the formation of acetic acid was not a lim-
iting step in producing methane. In this case, the similarly equal
richness of methanation-associated microbes and metagenomes
observed in both sludge and bioﬁlm indicates methanogenesis
was widely built up in the whole reactor. Further methane oxida-
tion was also strongly evidenced by accurately probing of genus
Methylogaea and genes (mmo and mox) with the potential AMO
capacity based on metagenome results. Instead of homogeneous
methanation, however, it was interesting to note that AMO was
overwhelmingly developed in the bioﬁlm. Why does AMO fail to
occur in the sludge bed with seemingly stronger methanogenesis
ability? We estimated that the setting of the packing bed as a ben-
eﬁcial habitat might prolong the contact time and enhance mass
transfer in the bulk liquid between methane and bioﬁlm, promot-
ing effective in situ capture of methane by methanotrophic bacte-
ria. Based on the abundance of key genes in AMO, methanol
might be a main ﬁnal byproduct, although the complete methane

These metagenomics ﬁndings positively proved that the coopera-
tiveinteractionofcore genomes ofmethanogens, aerobic methano-
trophs and denitriﬁers allowed SMAMOD to entirely removing COD
and nitrogen in the MUSBBRsystem. As for future application, one of
the most remarkable potentials in SMAMOD is in situ availability of
methane for easily cultivating aerobic methanotrophic microorgan-
isms in a methanogenic reactor, hence enhancing nitrogen removal
and relieving (dissolved) methane emission. Thus, it will offer a
promising and robust one-reactor process for sustainable treatment
of actual wastewaters such as chemical fertilizer, ﬁsh processing,
feeding and landﬁll leachate wastewater. By applying SMAMOD,
efﬁcient C and N removal with partial biogas recovery and GHG
reduction can be synergistically achieved. Yet, further SMAMOD
researches on rapid enrichment of AMB, acquirement of high-purity
methane using biogas separation techniques,42 novel bioreactor
exploitation for improving methane transfer and capture43 as well
as long-term optimization strategy will be still required.
CONCLUSION
In this study, a novel SMAMOD process achieving efﬁcient organic
and nitrogen removal as well as partial biogas recovery was devel-
oped in a single MUSBBR. The excellent performance was veriﬁed
by microbial community and gene proﬁling analysis. Functional
bacteria and functional genes were found to be involved in
methanogenesis, aerobic methane oxidation, and denitriﬁcation.
Genetic roadmap indicated complete pathways of aerobic/anaer-
obic fermentation, methane production, and methane aerobic
oxidation in organic metabolisms, while denitriﬁcation, DNRA,
assimilation nitrate reduction, and ﬁxed nitrogen pathways were
included in the nitrogen metabolism. Methanogenesis-, aerobic
methane oxidation-, and denitriﬁcation-associated metagenomic
cooperation and interaction led to SMAMOD.
